message.content:
The classic estimate for the size of the chess position space is called **Shannon’s number**. It was first proposed by Claude Shannon in 1950 and is usually quoted as:

\[
N_{\text{shannon}} \approx 10^{43}
\]

This figure represents an upper bound on the number of *legal* positions that can arise in a standard game of chess (i.e., positions that respect all rules such as piece counts, pawn placement, castling rights, etc.). More recent computational studies have refined this estimate slightly upward, but it still remains in the ballpark of \(10^{43}\)–\(10^{44}\).

So, when people say there are “about \(10^{43}\) possible arrangements” in chess, they’re referring to this well‑known Shannon number.
